How Tide Pools Work

By A. Writer

A tide pool is a shallow basin of seawater left behind on a rocky shore when the tide goes out. Twice a day the ocean floods it and drains away again, and everything living in it has to cope with the change.

The animals that do best are the ones that can hold on. A barnacle cements its head to the rock and spends its whole adult life there, kicking food into its shell with feathery legs whenever the water returns.

Snails and limpets graze on the thin film of algae that coats the stone. A limpet returns to the same scar on the rock after every trip, and its shell grows to fit that one spot exactly, which seals in moisture at low tide.

Sea stars move slowly on hundreds of tube feet. They pry open mussels with steady pressure, then push their stomach into the gap to digest the mussel in its own shell, a strategy that takes patience rather than speed.

Living with the tide

Temperature is the hardest test. On a sunny afternoon the water in a small pool can warm by ten degrees in an hour, while the oxygen in it falls. Animals that cannot leave close up, slow down and wait for the sea.

Salinity changes too. Rain dilutes a pool and evaporation concentrates it, so the same basin can swing from nearly fresh to saltier than the open ocean within a single day. Anemones pull in their tentacles and ride it out.

The pools higher up the shore are flooded for the shortest time and hold the hardiest species. Lower pools, covered for most of the day, are richer and more crowded, and competition for space there is fierce.

If you visit, step only on bare rock, turn any stone you lift back the way you found it, and leave every animal where it lives. A pool that took a season to settle can be disturbed in a minute.
